title: the mountain ahead
hook: the mountain ahead; Nanak's morning prayer

segments.voice: Yesterday: the Guru Granth Sahib. Your line was a living book. Today, the poem it opens with, and the last day of camp one.
screen: `THE GURU GRANTH SAHIB — A LIVING BOOK.` → `DAY 21.`

segments.voice: It's still dark outside. Four in the morning, maybe five. In homes in Punjab, London, Toronto, California and Nairobi, someone is already up. They've bathed. They sit quietly, cover their head, and begin to recite a long poem, often from memory. Some learned it as children, a verse at a time, beside a grandparent before school. It's the first thing in the scripture and the first thing in their day.
screen: `FOUR IN THE MORNING.` → `A LONG POEM, FROM MEMORY.` → `THE FIRST THING IN THE DAY.`

segments.voice: Japji Sahib. Jap, to recite, the same root as naam japna. Ji and Sahib, words of love and respect. It's Guru Nanak's great poem, and it opens the Guru Granth Sahib. It begins with the root verse from days ten and eleven. Then a short verse that the translator Macauliffe gave like this: "The True One was in the beginning; the True One was in the primal age." Then come thirty-eight stanzas, called pauris, steps or rungs, like a ladder, and a closing verse that pictures air as the Guru, water as the father, and the earth as the great mother of all. Inside, it's full of questions. Can you think your way to God? Not if you think a hundred thousand times, the first stanza says. What will do it? Living within hukam, God's will, the word from day seventeen. It's the first of the daily prayers, and nobody has to start with all of it: many begin with the root verse, then a stanza, then a little more. That's why your line is a promise. Later on this path, we'll climb Japji verse by verse. And look how far you've come. Waheguru, langar, the turban, the Panj Pyare, Ardas, Sikh, the Khanda. Seva, Ik Onkar, the root verse, both lines, kirat karni, vand chakna, naam japna. Sangat, the gurdwara, chardi kala, the five Ks, Guru Gobind Singh, the Guru Granth Sahib. And now Japji. Twenty-one words. Camp one is done.
screen: `JAP — TO RECITE.` · `THE TRUE ONE WAS IN THE BEGINNING.` · `THIRTY-EIGHT STEPS, LIKE A LADDER.` · `TWENTY-ONE WORDS. CAMP ONE DONE.`

segments.voice: Sit tall, the way someone sits in the early morning to recite. Picture a mountain path ahead of you, thirty-eight steps rising into the light. You don't have to climb today. Just stand at the bottom and look up. Then look back down the path you've already walked: twenty-one days, twenty-one words. Breathe with both, what's behind and what's ahead.
Japji Sahib. Guru Nanak's morning poem, the first in the scripture: the root verse, thirty-eight stanzas and a closing verse. Twenty-first word.
screen: `JAPJI SAHIB — your 21st word` → the strand complete → `CAMP ONE. DONE.`

segments.voice: Your line: 38 stanzas, verse by verse. One rung at a time, starting whenever you like. Tomorrow camp two begins: the stories, starting with a baby born in a small village in 1469.

screen: `DAY 21 COUNTS.` → `CAMP ONE COMPLETE.` → `TOMORROW: BORN AT TALWANDI, 1469.`

howItsDone: Sikhs who keep the daily prayers (Nitnem) recite Japji Sahib each morning, often before dawn after bathing, as the first of them; children often learn it by heart a stanza at a time.

fork.setup: you want to reach God. the first stanza of Japji weighs your options. which one does it point to?
options: think about it a hundred thousand times.
fork.reveal: thinking won't do it, silence won't, possessions won't. the stanza's answer is walking in the way of hukam.

original.note: Punjabi, in Gurmukhi script: jap, the title of the poem in the scripture; Japji Sahib adds words of respect.

trapdoor: what you thought: a long Sikh prayer.
what it means: Guru Nanak's morning poem, the first in the scripture: the root verse, thirty-eight stanzas and a closing verse, climbed like a ladder.

what a scholar hears: in the scripture its title is simply Jap. its stanzas are pauris, a word that also means rungs or steps, and it's recited in the morning as part of the daily prayers, the Nitnem.
